caseStudy.problem: Agents in ZeroClaw, OpenClaw, and other frameworks expose different interfaces. Eyrie's goal is to manage their projects, sessions, and lifecycle from a shared local control room, with a hierarchy of commanders, captains, and specialist talons.
caseStudy.built: I built the Go command-line application and React dashboard for agent discovery, lifecycle controls, project hierarchies, and streaming chat. Framework adapters translate a shared agent interface into each framework's gateway calls.
caseStudy.architecture: The CLI and dashboard share the adapter and discovery core. The Go executable embeds the built React application. SSE carries live updates; adapters use framework-specific HTTP or WebSocket connections. Configuration and project stores use local files, with SQLite used for ZeroClaw session access.
caseStudy.limitations: The approved captures show an empty first run. Live agent lifecycle, LLM chat, terminal sessions, and provisioning were not verified. Eyrie is an early local-only alpha with no authentication; it is not a hosted multi-user service.

diagram.title: Simplified local architecture
diagram.summary: The React dashboard exchanges HTTP requests, server-sent events, and terminal WebSocket traffic with a local Go server. The server uses discovery and framework adapters to reach agent runtimes. Project and instance data use local JSON files. The ZeroClaw adapter can read session history from SQLite.
description: The Go executable embeds the built React dashboard. The browser calls its HTTP API, receives server-sent events, and connects to terminal sessions over WebSocket. The paired arrows show requests and responses.

Discovery finds configured agents and probes their health. Adapters expose a shared Agent interface for framework-specific operations. The command-line interface also uses discovery and lifecycle controls.
Projects and instances use local JSON files. The ZeroClaw adapter can also read session history directly from a local SQLite database, including when the gateway is unavailable.
diagram.caveat: This diagram shows selected paths in the source. Live agent workflows remain unverified. Eyrie is a local-only alpha without authentication.

caseStudy.problem: swift-ship explores an AI-assisted customer support desk that combines ticket handling, knowledge search, and customer conversations. Its source also includes freight estimates and shipment tracking.
caseStudy.built: I built a support prototype with ticket queues, replies and internal notes, knowledge editing, and customer portal pages. The AI chat routes requests to support, documentation, quote, or shipment agents. These capabilities are present in source; their authenticated behavior remains unverified.
caseStudy.architecture: Next.js pages and API handlers use service modules backed by Supabase Auth, PostgreSQL, and Realtime. The AI route forwards responses from Supabase Edge Functions as server-sent events. Documentation search uses OpenAI embeddings and a pgvector database query.
caseStudy.limitations: The public link shows sign-in only. The production build used placeholder service configuration and skips TypeScript and lint checks; those checks and the tests fail separately. The checked-in migrations are not a verified fresh-database setup. Login, ticket operations, and AI responses still need functional verification.

diagram.title: Simplified AI request path
diagram.summary: The React support interface sends chat messages to the Next.js AI support API. The API forwards requests to one of four Supabase Edge Functions and relays server-sent events to the browser. The functions call OpenAI. The documentation agent also retrieves matching content from PostgreSQL with pgvector.
description: The browser sends chat messages to the Next.js AI support route. That route forwards the request to a support, documentation, quote, or shipment Edge Function and relays its server-sent events. Paired arrows show requests and responses.
The documentation agent creates an OpenAI embedding of the query, retrieves matching content through the PostgreSQL match_embeddings function, and uses that content in an OpenAI chat completion.
This view follows the main AI route. Ticket services, Supabase Auth, and Realtime are separate application paths. A second agent implementation also exists inside the Next.js codebase.

title: codex-video-vision
oneLiner: Video tools for Codex. A credited port of an MIT-licensed project.
description: A Codex video tool server using MCP, TypeScript, and ffmpeg.
verificationNote: Eyrie reported 108 passing tests on October 29, 2026. This is a credited port of an MIT-licensed project. No live demo or end-to-end transcription check is claimed.
notes: Evidence: portfolio-brief/v2/verified-projects.md. Preserve the credited-port attribution.

caseStudy.problem: A coding agent needs timestamped frames and audio information to inspect a local video. This project prepares metadata, images, scene analysis, and optional transcripts for the agent to interpret.
caseStudy.built: I adapted the MIT-licensed claude-video-vision project for Codex, preserving its upstream credit and license. The port includes a local MCP server and workflows for video inspection and storyboard comparison.
caseStudy.architecture: A TypeScript server exposes MCP tools for metadata, analysis, frame extraction, and closer inspection of selected timestamps. ffmpeg and ffprobe process local media. A session cache supports later frame retrieval. Transcription can use Gemini, OpenAI Whisper, or a local Whisper backend.
caseStudy.limitations: Transcription tests use mocked backends; real API transcription and local Whisper inference were not verified. Codex Desktop plugin discovery and long-video performance also remain unchecked. The report validates the local source build, not a published npm installation or a hosted demo.

title: ChatGenius
description: A chat application built with React, Supabase, FastAPI, and pgvector. Code only; no public demo is linked.
verificationNote: Eyrie reported all 55 frontend tests passing on October 29, 2026. Backend services and a live chat flow are not verified here. Code only; no demo link.
notes: Evidence: portfolio-brief/v2/verified-projects.md supersedes the earlier demo-down seed. Do not restore old demo links.

caseStudy.problem: ChatGenius explores Slack-like communication with channels, direct messages, attachments, and AI replies based on message history. It combines the chat interface and AI response paths in one codebase.
caseStudy.built: I built a React chat frontend and a Python API for AI replies and related chat operations. The source includes channel and direct-message organization, presence, threads, and file sharing. This portfolio presents the code only, without a live demo.
caseStudy.architecture: The application lives in frontend/ and backend/; the root React starter is separate. The frontend uses Supabase for authentication, data, and live updates. FastAPI chat routes retrieve Supabase message history and call OpenAI directly. A separate SQLAlchemy package implements vector retrieval with PostgreSQL and pgvector.
caseStudy.limitations: The passing frontend tests do not establish full type correctness or a working chat service. Standalone type checking fails, backend tests fail before assertions, and database migrations need reconciliation. Authenticated messaging, uploads, and AI replies remain unverified.
